changes.before: Figures S5-S6 show the weak dypingite diffraction feature, platy coating and Mg-C-bearing EDS interaction volumes. The small sample and very low carbonate abundance prevented quantitative phase analysis. Silicon and sodium in EDS may include underlying clay. Table S6 reports lower, not higher, Mg weight percentage in the coating volume than the starting clay; the main text’s Mg-enrichment wording is therefore not adopted.
changes.after: Figures S5 and S6 show the weak dypingite diffraction feature and Mg-C-bearing EDS interaction volumes, respectively; the platy coating morphology is shown in main Figure 5. The small sample and very low carbonate abundance prevented quantitative phase analysis. Silicon and sodium in EDS may include underlying clay. The EDS concentration inset in Figure S6 reports lower, not higher, Mg weight percentage in the coating volume than the starting clay; the main text’s Mg-enrichment wording is therefore not adopted.

changes.before: Sections 3.1 and 4.1 assign likely stevensite using broad diffraction, a 1.53 angstrom 060 reflection, Mg/Si 0.73 and treated basal-spacing changes: 13.95 to 14.53 angstrom with ethylene glycol, and 12.32 after heating and glycol treatment. These support the authors’ poorly crystalline smectite interpretation, not a refined pure-phase identification. Section 4.3 proposes photosynthesis, heterotrophy and EPS effects but does not separately measure those causal contributions; borosilicate vessels may also supply silicon.
changes.after: Section 3.1 assigns likely stevensite using broad diffraction, a 1.53 angstrom 060 reflection, Mg/Si 0.73 and treated basal-spacing changes: 13.95 to 14.53 angstrom with ethylene glycol, and 12.32 after heating and glycol treatment. Section 4.1 proposes photosynthesis, heterotrophy and EPS effects but does not separately measure those causal contributions; Section 4.3 notes that borosilicate vessels may also supply silicon.

changes.before: Figures S1-S4 and Table S1 corroborate starting-material morphology, treated diffraction and solution sampling. Quartz is attributed to preparation contamination. Evaporation and sampling complicate concentration comparisons. Main Tables 3 and 4 reverse the final BIO3/BIO3null Mg values (0.70 and 0.95 mmol/L), so no quantitative Mg-removal efficiency or clay-specific carbonate yield is adopted. Theoretical carbon-storage capacity and modeled saturation are not measured capture.
changes.after: Figures S1-S4 document treated natural/synthetic clay diffraction, biotic bottle photographs and abiotic solid diffraction; Table S1 characterizes digested synthetic clay. Tables S2-S3 contain the abiotic and biotic solution measurements. Quartz is attributed to preparation contamination. Evaporation and sampling complicate concentration comparisons. Main Tables 3 and 4 reverse the final BIO3/BIO3null Mg values (0.70 and 0.95 mmol/L), so no quantitative Mg-removal efficiency or clay-specific carbonate yield is adopted. Theoretical carbon-storage capacity and modeled saturation are not measured capture.
